text:
Recent work supports evaluating individual claims against evidence rather than relying on semantic similarity. A 2025/2026 recommendation study reports BERTScore F1 of 0.81–0.90 alongside statement-level factual precision of only 4.38%–32.88%; its review-derived evidence is unavailable in this task, but its atomic-claim evaluation approach transfers. [Factual Consistency](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24366). The 2026 SimInter preprint audits simulated-user claims against historical conversations and reports 94.3% supported or partially supported claims; this does not establish that inferred traits are observable in interaction-only histories. [SimInter](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18308).

Suggested adaptation: annotate each actual feedback claim with user/item IDs, the exact feedback span, supporting history events, and title/description spans. Separate explicit specification conflicts, functional similarity, and insufficient information. A stated connector mismatch can support a compatibility conflict; similar titles alone cannot establish redundancy, ownership, compatibility, or unmet need. Missing specifications require abstention. Keep simulator-generated complaints identified as simulated observations, without treating them as verified real-user preferences.

Validate the rubric on independently annotated examples before adjudication. Report raw agreement and Cohen’s kappa or Krippendorff’s alpha, label frequencies, evidence-span agreement, and abstention rates with explicit denominators. Preserve disagreements and reasons; a 2025 annotation study finds that task formulation and annotator choice change instance-level labels even when overall agreement remains similar. [Sources of Disagreement](https://aclanthology.org/2025.comedi-1.3/). These are proposed diagnostic procedures, not measured results for this benchmark. Keep the twenty simulator users descriptive and retain official macro validation HR@10 as the model-selection criterion.
